cover.note: We are opening the Elegex Phase 2 audit with a strict mandate on evidence over claims. We must distinguish between what is rendered in the UI and what can be proven at the database and transaction level. Let's make sure our technical assessments rest strictly on verified execution. And this sets the tone for every subsequent review in the deck.

evidence_reset.note: The audit forced us to confront a direct contradiction between our prior acceptance reports and our actual reference UX analysis. We cannot claim a field service lifecycle is complete when the underlying transactional reality is missing. Evidence, not a rendered route, determines acceptance. Let's look at how the foreman ground truth exposes this gap.

foreman_ground_truth.note: When we test the foreman journey against actual execution, the gaps are stark. Almost every critical step, from geolocation check-in to signature capture and sync queue drain, is completely absent. Only the foreman job card shows partial capability. But partial schema support does not mean an accepted workflow. Let's examine how this realization forced a formal retraction.

acceptance_retraction.note: We had to retract and reissue our final acceptance because manual observation of rendered routes stood in for functional verification. We did not record complete authenticated journeys or prove the resulting table writes. And that is governance failure we cannot repeat. The workflow remains firmly in our active implementation backlog. Let's move into how WP2 begins restoring the proper domain context to fix these foundational gaps.

wp2_domain.note: Work Package 2 moves us away from generic USD defaults and into the real operating context of a South African electrical contractor. We are embedding local currency, timezone settings, and temporal call-out types directly into the organization model. But remember, this is a schema and migration foundation only. User-facing settings controls still require subsequent implementation and verification. Let's transition into how our domain schema enforces these commercial relationships.

domain_schema.note: We need a schema that mirrors the commercial reality of South African electrical contracting rather than forcing everything into a generic contact record. We mapped specific business needs directly to our database design, separating temporal call-out rates, billing entities from site contacts, and multi-location service sites. Building on the domain foundations we just established, these new tenant-scoped tables and job references give us the exact structure required for our operations. Notice that we didn't just add columns; we created a proper taxonomy for call-out types that handles base rates, kilometers, and service windows safely. This is a foundational step, and we still need to enforce historical rate behavior and expose these settings in our actual user flows.

migration_foundation.note: Our migration strategy for WP2 is deliberately additive so we never destructively reprice or overwrite existing jobs. Migration 0008 introduces our new domain tables and extends organization settings without breaking historical records. Following the schema design we just reviewed, every new job reference is nullable to ensure a job priced in March keeps its exact March rate. We added tenant-scoped call-out types, clients, and sites while linking jobs directly to their proper operating contexts. This gives us a solid foundation for the offline sync architecture we are building next.

offline_gap.note: We must be honest about our current state because UI optimism is not an offline guarantee. The existing foreman experience relies entirely on direct server mutations with zero offline protection. Building on the data model foundations we just put in place, we now have to address a glaring vulnerability in the field. Right now, there is no IndexedDB queue to survive an app kill or a device reboot. There are no client-generated idempotency keys, and there is no dependency enforcement. A simple network drop in the field will prevent work from being persisted, which means we have a lot of work ahead in WP5.

offline_architecture.note: To solve our offline gaps, our mobile architecture must make every piece of field work durable before touching the network. Building directly on the persistence problem we just outlined, our target design relies on a strict write-ahead pattern. Every mutation gets enqueued in IndexedDB first so it survives device reboots and force quits. We assign client-generated UUIDs to every operation to guarantee idempotency on the server side. We also enforce causal dependencies, ensuring check-ins happen before materials, and materials happen before job completion. Binary data like photos and signatures stay as local blobs instead of data URLs to protect device memory. When the network returns, the sync engine drains these operations safely and in order.

queue_controls.note: And moving from our architecture design to runtime mechanics, we have to look closely at queue safety controls. Offline safety isn't solved by a simple retry button. It demands a coordinated set of persistence, ordering, binary, and failure-management rules. Every item in the queue must protect field work from network drops, duplicate replays, and silent data loss. When we talk about interrupted networks, we rely on exponential backoff with jitter and capped retries. Replay protection uses client-generated UUIDs with server-side deduplication against organization and key. Causality matters deeply here. We enforce strict dependency graphs where check-ins precede materials, and evidence precedes completion. Binary data like photos and signatures are stored as raw blobs in IndexedDB rather than bloated base64 strings. And when a mutation hits permanent failure, it surfaces an actionable item instead of being silently dropped. We must ensure that replaying a completed queue yields zero duplicate rows while strictly preserving causal order.

implementation_path.note: Building on these queue mechanics, our implementation path follows a strictly ordered delivery schedule. Later experience claims depend directly on the persistence, document structure, tenant isolation, and test evidence we establish first. We build the database and domain foundation before proving that every field artifact is durable and isolated. Package two deploys our schema foundation for locales, currencies, timezones, and temporal call-out types. Package four introduces typed, governed documents and verifies routing and tenant isolation. Package five implements the IndexedDB write-ahead queue, idempotency keys, and blob uploads. Finally, packages nine and ten run adversarial proofs and validate authenticated journeys in end-to-end coverage. Our release rule remains absolute. Each package stays marked incomplete until both its implementation and its named verification artifact exist in the repository.

closing.note: Bringing this all together, our closing standard anchors everything in functional proof. This audit refuses to certify unfinished work. Instead, it establishes ground truth, a robust domain foundation, and the strict standard by which future delivery will be measured. We must build the real workflow and leave behind decorative controls where tenant-scoped persistence is missing. We record concrete evidence through execution logs, resulting database writes, adversarial checks, and automated browser runs. We accept only verified work because rendered routes, schema declarations, and assertions of completion are never substitutes for empirical proof. Functional verification remains our only valid path to credible acceptance.
